newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE - Massacre shifted Australians on gun rights.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Massacre shifted Australians on gun rights.

text.p: The gun massacre of 35 people at the quiet Australian tourist site of Port Arthur a year ago sent the nation into deep shock, but also left one important legacy.
The killings last April 28 galvanised Australia's politicians -- state, territory and federal -- to take on the politically powerful gun lobby and launch an historic crackdown on gun ownership.
Conservative prime minister John Howard personally led the crusade to outlaw hundreds of thousands of guns -- a move widely regarded as the greatest achievement of his first year in power.

Howard was elected barely a month before social misfit Martin Bryant opened fire with semi-automatic weapons at the popular tourist site and former penal colony in the southern island state of Tasmania, committing modern Australia's worst mass murder.

"The tightening of the gun laws was one of the very few positive things that flowed out of the massacre," National Coalition for Gun Control deputy chairman Roland Browne told Reuters by telephone from his home in Tasmania.
"But I'd like it to be acknowledged that the tightening of our gun laws came at a tremendous cost to the community, especially in Tasmania," he said.
PRO-GUN LOBBY STAGE MASS PROTESTS

Despite overwhelming public support for Howard's crusade to ban and buy back high-powered and rapid-fire rifles from civilians, pro-gun groups have staged mass protests in streets and country halls around the nation.

Some of the more extreme groups have threatened a civil uprising against what they labelled a totalitarian regime bent on snatching their right to bear arms, warning their freedom would be regained with blood.
"The only currency you can purchase freedom back with is blood -- that's the only currency," Firearms Owners Association president Ian McNiven told a rally in conservative Queensland state last year.

The intensity of the pro-gun lobby's campaign prompted authorities to boost security for key politicians and to force Howard to wear a bullet-proof vest at a pro-gun protest -- an unprecedented precaution in a country where security for even the prime minister is usually minimal.
Howard's Liberal-National coalition government and allied state governments also faced a backlash from their rural heartland, where farmers regard guns as everyday work tools.
DIVISIONS FADE AS ANNIVERSARY NEARS

But as the first anniversary of the massacre approaches, the divisions have faded and the six state and two territory governments, which are responsible for gun laws, have all passed laws imposing Howard's crackdown.
However, the laws have yet to come fully into force in some states.

An A$500 million-a-year (US$387.5 million) government buyback scheme, funded by an average A$70 annual levy on all taxpayers, has so far seen almost 400,000 guns handed in to authorities, at a cost of A$190 million.
Authorities are destroying almost all the guns handed in, although a few of historical value are going to museums.
But the gun control lobby warns more needs to be done to prevent another Port Arthur, pointing to what it says is a gaping hole in laws controlling pistols.
"High-powered semi-automatic hand guns are still legally available in this country," the gun control lobby's Browne said.
"It's an anomaly that was overlooked when the changes to the law were passed last year.

"What's significant is that in Britain in 1996, it was a high-powered semi-automatic hand gun that Thomas Hamilton used at Dunblane, so the scenario that existed in Britain in March 1996 is still in place in Australia."
Hamilton gunned down 16 children and their teacher in a school gymnasium in the Scottish village of Dunblane on March 13 last year, a few weeks before the Port Arthur killings.
DUNBLANE FATHERS COMMEMORATE PORT ARTHUR SLAYINGS

The fathers of three children murdered at Dunblane have travelled to Tasmania for the Port Arthur anniversary, to meet relatives of the victims, help record a song about the two massacres and campaign for further gun law reform.

"The hand gun law in Australia is as it was (in Britain) on March 13 last year and that means that any person armed to the teeth could do something unpredictable," said Les Morton, whose five-year-old daughter, Emily, was killed at Dunblane.
Morton rejected civil liberties arguments for gun ownership.
"Unfortunately, our daughters don't have civil liberties anymore -- they were taken away by a man with a gun," he said.
